## New React DOM Features

- `browser()`: a new `react-dom` API that returns a usable which errors during server rendering and resolves in the browser. `use(browser())` inside a `<Suspense>` boundary marks a subtree as browser-only without reporting a recoverable error (@gnoff: [#37143](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/37143), [#37241](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/37241))
  - Added an `onBrowserBailout` option to the `react-dom/server` APIs to observe when a subtree defers to the browser (@gnoff [#37193](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/37193))

## Notable changes

- Enable Trusted Types API integration (@rickhanlonii [#35816](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/35816))
- Transitions now render independently instead of being entangled into a single render, so a slow transition no longer holds up unrelated ones (@acdlite [#37290](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/37290))
- Added a DEV-only warning when a component appears to have been unblocked by calling `use()` conditionally (@hoxyq, @eps1lon: [#37104](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/37104), [#37203](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/37203), [#37491](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/37491))

### React

  - Unify hot reload type resolution for Fast Refresh (@sophiebits [#36962](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/36962))
  - Fix Fast Refresh to remount correctly when an edit changes the component kind (@sophiebits [#36950](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/36950))

issue.title: [React 19] Reintroduce debugSource in some kind of opt-in way
issue.body: ## Summary `__debugSource` was removed in #28265 to solve problems that do not apply to us and without including any 1:1 replacement that we could make work for our case. We are currently looking for ways to re-implement it for React 19 but all approaches seem quite hacky or fragile without any additional support from React. We use `__debugSource` to create a mapping between a DOM element (fiber node in practice) to the source location where the JSX element was created. We use this information to be able to implement an in-browser, in-app editor for JSX, e.g. we can find a fiber node from a DOM element and then find the exact source location where the element was created, parse the file and modify the JSX node. Naturally, this is only ever available in dev mode. We control the main configuration for how TSX/JSX is transformed into JS so getting accurate source information has never been a problem. However, all approaches using stack traces and similar will not work as they only contain the line number and not exact location in the source file. Take for instance the JSX code ```jsx function MyView() { return <>HelloHelloHello; } ``` and it is quite difficult to know which element a `` from the DOM maps to, even if the line number is available. We have prototyped some workarounds like using our own jsx dev transform and placing the source info manually somewhere but these approaches also have issues: 1. If placing on the `ReactElement`, we have to abuse an existing property as only those are copied to the fiber nodes when rendering. The closest one would be `_debugInfo` but that will probably be overwritten in some cases 2. Placing the mapping in a global variable would work but as only the `ReactElement` instance is available at that point, and that instance is not referenced from a fiber node, there does not seem to be anything sensible available to use as a key for the map We could rewrite part of the React code but that would seem even more fragile. Good ideas are welcome

issue.title: [DOM] Use a separate marker for the document selectionchange listener
issue.body:
## Summary

Fixes #37695

`listenToAllSupportedEvents` used the same `listeningMarker` for the root container and for the document level `selectionchange` listener. When the root is the document (which is what Next.js App Router does), the marker is already set by the time we get to selectionchange, so it never gets added and onSelect misses selection changes that only come through selectionchange. And if another root ran first, the document already has the marker, so a later document root skips all of its listeners and onClick etc never fire.

I gave selectionchange its own marker so the two dont step on each other. The existing "should not subscribe to selectionchange twice" test still covers the dedupe.

## How did you test this change?

Added three tests to ReactDOMEventListener-test.js: a document root subscribes to selectionchange, onSelect fires on selectionchange with a document root, and a document root still gets clicks when another root was created first. All three fail on main and pass with this change.

- `yarn test ReactDOMEventListener` and `yarn test --prod ReactDOMEventListener`: 26 passed

issue.title: Bug: document roots never get the selectionchange listener, and lose all events if another root was created first
issue.body:
React version: 19.3.0-canary-d083ec1d-20260922 (same code on main)

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Mount React on the whole document instead of a div, with `createRoot(document)` or `hydrateRoot(document, <App />)`. This is what Next.js App Router does, so every App Router app is set up this way.
2. Render a text input with an `onSelect` handler and focus it.
3. Change the selection in a way that doesnt come with a key or mouse event, for example calling `input.setSelectionRange(0, 5)` from code, or dragging the selection handles on a phone.
4. onSelect never fires. The exact same input mounted on a normal div root does fire.

Those selection changes only come through `selectionchange`, and a document root never gets a `selectionchange` listener, so React never sees them.

There is also a worse version of this. If any other React root was created on the page before the document root, the document root doesnt get any event listeners at all, so even clicks stop working.

Link to code example:

```jsx
// another root created first, e.g. a widget some library mounts
createRoot(document.createElement('div')).render(<span />);

createRoot(document).render(
  <html>
    <body>
      <button onClick={() => console.log('clicked')}>click me</button>
    </body>
  </html>
);
// clicking the button logs nothing
```

## The current behavior

In `listenToAllSupportedEvents` (DOMPluginEventSystem.js) the same `listeningMarker` is used for two things: "this root already has its listeners" and "this document already has the selectionchange listener". When the root is the document itself, the marker gets set on it right before the selectionchange check, so that check thinks its already done and skips it. And if a div root runs first it puts the marker on the document for selectionchange, so a later document root thinks its already listening and skips everything.

## The expected behavior

A document root gets the selectionchange listener like a div root does, and the order roots are created in shouldnt matter. I have a small fix with tests (a separate marker for selectionchange) and will open a PR.

issue.body:
### What kind of issue is this?

- [x] React Compiler core (the JS output is incorrect, or your app works incorrectly after optimization)
- [ ] babel-plugin-react-compiler (build issue installing or using the Babel plugin)
- [ ] eslint-plugin-react-hooks (build issue installing or using the eslint plugin)
- [ ] react-compiler-healthcheck (build issue installing or using the healthcheck script)

### Link to repro

https://github.com/kbitgood/rc-bug-repro-increment-assign

### Repro steps

#### Description
When using the post increment operator in an assignment (`y = x++`) the value is incremented before being assigned when using the React Compiler.
 
#### Steps to Reproduce
1. Check out the reproduction repository
2. Run `npm run dev`, or `npm run build && npm run start` as the problem exists in both dev mode and production
3. See the index field of each item in the next list is off by one. Every item in the list should have a sequential "Count" value starting at 1, not

#### Details in the Reproduction Code
The code in `src/app/page.tsx` uses Array.reduce to build an array of nodes, and keeps track of a counter in the aggregated value. 

When we use this code:
```ts
const count = agg.itemCounter++;
```
The compiled output translates to:
```ts
agg.itemCounter = agg.itemCounter + 1;
const count = agg.itemCounter;
```
Which is not equivalent because it increments before assigning, rather than assigning and then incrementing.

The issue goes away by taking the counter out of the aggregate object and into a normal variable outside of the reduce function. 

#### Conclusion
I realize that this way of keeping the count in the aggregated value is not the best way, but this is not strictly against the "Rules of React". If it is, it should probably be added to the ESLint rules. 

This issue was found on a large codebase that was working just fine before enabling the compiler. And we had no indication that this code would not work after enabling the compiler.

Every time

19.2.0

issue.title: Preserve SSR Suspense fallback across client re-suspend (#37620)
issue.body:
﻿## Summary
- Fixes https://github.com/react/react/issues/37620 (BountyHub `$100`): when `use(browser())` leaves a permanent SSR Suspense fallback and hydration re-suspends on a client-created promise (`setTimeout` / `localStorage` / IndexedDB shape), keep the dehydrated fallback DOM mounted instead of deleting and remounting an identical fallback.
- Remounting restarted CSS animations (Progress) and dropped DOM state even though the visible UI looked unchanged.
- Gate is tight to the recoverable `browser()` digest so ordinary error fallbacks still take the existing client-render path.

## Implementation
In `updateDehydratedSuspenseComponent`, when a permanent fallback re-suspends on the client:
1. Drop the dehydrated fragment from pending deletions.
2. Mount a hidden primary Offscreen fiber for the retry.
3. Reuse the existing dehydrated fallback sibling instead of creating a new fallback fragment.

Also teach `updateSuspenseFallbackChildren` / `bailoutOffscreenComponent` not to treat a preserved `DehydratedFragment` as renderable children.

## Test plan
- [x] `yarn test --build=false ReactDOMFizzServer-test --testNamePattern="browser-only|does not remount|replaces the SSR|keeps the SSR fallback"` → **7 passed**
- [x] New regression: client promise after `use(browser())` keeps the same `<span>` node identity across hydration
- [x] Control: hydration that finishes without re-suspending still replaces the SSR fallback
- [x] Multi-suspend: fallback identity preserved across sequential client promises

## Bounty
Claiming the BountyHub bounty on #37620.

issue.title: [React 19] Reintroduce debugSource in some kind of opt-in way
issue.body: ## Summary `__debugSource` was removed in #28265 to solve problems that do not apply to us and without including any 1:1 replacement that we could make work for our case. We are currently looking for ways to re-implement it for React 19 but all approaches seem quite hacky or fragile without any additional support from React. We use `__debugSource` to create a mapping between a DOM element (fiber node in practice) to the source location where the JSX element was created. We use this information to be able to implement an in-browser, in-app editor for JSX, e.g. we can find a fiber node from a DOM element and then find the exact source location where the element was created, parse the file and modify the JSX node. Naturally, this is only ever available in dev mode. We control the main configuration for how TSX/JSX is transformed into JS so getting accurate source information has never been a problem. However, all approaches using stack traces and similar will not work as they only contain the line number and not exact location in the source file. Take for instance the JSX code ```jsx function MyView() { return <>HelloHelloHello; } ``` and it is quite difficult to know which element a `` from the DOM maps to, even if the line number is available. We have prototyped some workarounds like using our own jsx dev transform and placing the source info manually somewhere but these approaches also have issues: 1. If placing on the `ReactElement`, we have to abuse an existing property as only those are copied to the fiber nodes when rendering. The closest one would be `_debugInfo` but that will probably be overwritten in some cases 2. Placing the mapping in a global variable would work but as only the `ReactElement` instance is available at that point, and that instance is not referenced from a fiber node, there does not seem to be anything sensible available to use as a key for the map We could rewrite part of the React code but that would seem even more fragile. Good ideas are welcome

We use this information to be able to implement an in-browser, in-app editor for JSX, e.g. we can find a fiber node from a DOM element and then find the exact source location where the element was created, parse the file and modify the JSX node. Naturally, this is only ever available in dev mode. We control the main configuration for how TSX/JSX is transformed into JS so getting accurate source information has never been a problem. However, all approaches using stack traces and similar will not work as they only contain the line number and not exact location in the source file. Take for instance the JSX code ```jsx function MyView() { return <>HelloHelloHello; } ``` and it is quite difficult to know which element a `` from the DOM maps to, even if the line number is available. We have prototyped some workarounds like using our own jsx dev transform and placing the source info manually somewhere but these approaches also have issues: 1. If placing on the `ReactElement`, we have to abuse an existing property as only those are copied to the fiber nodes when rendering. The closest one would be `_debugInfo` but that will probably be overwritten in some cases 2. Placing the mapping in a global variable would work but as only the `ReactElement` instance is available at that point, and that instance is not referenced from a fiber node, there does not seem to be anything sensible available to use as a key for the map We could rewrite part of the React code but that would seem even more fragile. Good ideas are welcome
